channel.title: Cameras Decoded — Blog & Updates
channel.description: Guides, gear breakdowns, and business advice for mirrorless operators — from Cameras Decoded.

item.title: What Ten Years With One Subject Can Teach You
item.description: Ivan McClellan first encountered Black rodeo culture in Oklahoma in 2015. A decade of returning built the relationships behind Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion, a book of more than 90 previously unpublished photographs.

item.title: Depth Is Not the Blur
item.description: Max Kent calls a wide aperture the lazy version of depth. His case: soft light from roughly 45 degrees above and to the side, plus a clear foreground, midground, and background, build separation that survives even at f/8.

item.title: Sigma Is Selling Character Now, Not Just Sharpness
item.description: Sigma's 50mm F1.4 CL DG Contemporary is the first in a new CL line: 65mm long, 375 grams, aluminum body, and soft corners by design. It arrives in early spring 2027 for L and Sony E mounts, with no price announced yet.

item.title: Blur Is the Shortcut. Depth Is the Skill.
item.description: Background blur is the shortcut everyone learns first. Photographer Max Kent argues that real depth comes from directional light and layered composition — and phones have been faking bokeh since 2016.

item.title: Old Glass, Sharper Photographer
item.description: Travis Butler shoots a Sigma fp and Lumix S5 with adapted film-era lenses. His reason is not nostalgia: a decade of manual focus forced him to truly understand aperture and the focal plane.

item.title: The Finish Is a Decision
item.description: Lightroom on mobile can now open closed eyes and expand your photos with generative AI. Useful tools — and a test of honesty, because one of them invents parts of your photograph.

item.title: The App That Won't Let You Chimp
item.description: Documentary photographer Dennis Berti built WorthWait, an iPhone camera app that hides your photos for 24 hours. The wait is the entire point.

item.title: Nobody Looks Good Being Watched
item.description: Portrait photographer Julia Trotti shares her method for keeping non-models relaxed in front of the camera: comfortable distance, short sessions, and loose direction.

item.title: Sony Gave Your Telephoto Lens a Memory
item.description: Firmware 1.02 for the Sony A7R VI extends Preset Focus to non-power-zoom lenses: save a focus distance, snap back to it with one button press.

item.title: The Most Important Camera Setting You're Probably Not Using
item.description: C1, C2 and C3 sit on your mode dial doing nothing. A working photographer argues they're the closest thing to a workflow game-changer he's found — here's how to put them to work.

item.title: 14 Landscape Photography Beliefs Worth Questioning
item.description: You don't need a wide angle, exotic travel, or a tripod everywhere. Michael Scott walks through the myths that quietly shape what beginners buy, where they go, and how they judge their progress.

item.title: Sony's 20-70mm f/4 Might Be the Mountain Zoom to Beat
item.description: Two lightweight Sony zooms went climbing to see which could replace a 24-70mm f/2.8. The wider one won — and AI denoising has quietly changed the f/4 math.

item.title: What a Star Timelapse Actually Teaches You About Gear
item.description: The iOptron SkyTracker Pro did its job — then a loose ball head sent it swinging, and it barely mattered. The takeaway from a night under New Mexico's new moon: your star timelapse needs less gear than you think.

item.title: How to Edit Autumn Foliage Without Overcooking It
item.description: Pit Haupert leaves the global saturation slider alone entirely. His autumn foliage workflow: texture up, clarity around minus 20, per-color mixer work, and RGB curves for warm highlights over cool shadows.

item.title: You Don't Need a Fiery Sunset to Make a Great Landscape Photo
item.description: Craig Roberts has stopped chasing epic light. His case: the pleasant, ordinary scenes near your door — shot often, learned deeply — make stronger photographers than one trip a year to a famous viewpoint.

item.title: Why In-Camera Presets Aren't Cheating
item.description: Fujifilm's film simulations, custom recipes on OM System and Nikon \u2014 Digital Camera World's Mike Harris argues in-camera presets aren't cheating. They teach exposure discipline, kill editing anxiety, and keep you shooting instead of sitting at a screen.

item.title: Your Stabilization Rating Comes From a Shaker Table, Not a Hand
item.description: Your camera's stabilization rating comes from a shaker table in a temperature-controlled room, not a human hand. The test is rigorous, but the focal length and lens are the manufacturer's choice \u2014 so 8.5 stops and 7.5 stops are not reliably a stop apart.

item.title: How to Find Compositions When the Location Overwhelms You
item.description: Omar Gonzalez fought the tourist-snapshot trap in Vermont and won. His answer: compositional blinders \u2014 the viewfinder, a long lens, or a crop mode that forces your eye to find the frame.

item.title: What Your First Print Will Teach You About Your Own Photos
item.description: A DPReview writer finally makes a real darkroom print of one of his favorite photos, and the physical print reveals things the screen never could.

item.title: How Far Can You Push Exposure Before Losing the Subject?
item.description: Wildlife photographer Somdutt Prasad overexposed his Hokkaido crane series \"beyond what felt natural\" and turned Japanese red-crowned cranes into ink-wash paintings.

item.title: Why Boredom Might Be the Best Thing for Your Street Photography
item.description: Street photography is 95% waiting, says Peter Forsgard. Learning to sit inside the slow hours is what sharpens your eye, and panic shots are where most bad images come from.

item.title: Turn Any Small Venue Into a Portrait Studio With One Light
item.description: Jiggie Alejandrino ran a 50-person portrait station in a small brand-launch venue with a single Profoto B10X Plus shaped into a book light. His 1/320s, f/2, ISO 100 recipe kills ambient light so the strobe does everything, and a foam-board version gets you close on a budget.

item.title: RAW Editing Just Moved Into Your Browser, Free to Start
item.description: Skylum launched Luminar on Web, a browser-based photo editor that handles RAW files. The basic version is free forever and full access is a one-time $69, a new low-friction doorway into real RAW editing for learners.

item.title: High Camera Prices Are Not Proof Camera Makers Are Greedy
item.description: DPReview's Dale Baskin argues that rising camera prices reflect real design and manufacturing costs, not greed. His reframe for buyers: stop asking why makers are greedy and ask whether the camera is worth it to you.

item.title: A 14-Year-Old Won Wildlife Photographer of the Year With a Dung Beetle
item.description: Oscar Whitfield's black-and-white Labour of Love proves the extraordinary hides inside the ordinary. His technique was humble: lie flat, get to eye level, and shoot fast.

item.title: Your Photography Website Needs One Job
item.description: Portfolio, print store, workshop hub, blog. One homepage cannot do all of those jobs well. The fix is a single question: what is the primary job this space is meant to do?

item.title: Every Flash Photo Is Really Two Exposures
item.description: Photographer JC Carey breaks flash down to a repeatable decision order: set the ambient with the camera, set the subject with the strobe, and never let the two argue.

item.title: A Rocket Left a Glowing 'Space Jellyfish' Over Florida. Here Is How to Catch the Next One
item.description: A SpaceX Falcon 9 launch this week painted a glowing 'space jellyfish' across the Florida sky, and NASA's photographers were ready. The phenomenon is predictable, which means you can plan for it: the same pad launches again Monday, October 19 at 6:30 AM.

item.title: An Award Only for Photographers Under Three Years In. These Winners Are Worth Studying
item.description: You do not need a decade behind the camera to make award-winning work. The AOP's Emerging Talent Awards, open only to photographers with less than three years of practice, just crowned a gold winner who rigged a 57-metre highline across a melting Icelandic glacier.

item.title: 1,500 Games In, the Cubs' Photographer Still Plans Every Frame Before It Happens
item.description: Matt Dirksen has shot more than 1,500 baseball games. The Cubs' team photographer explains how he reads light, predicts endings before each pitch, and delivers publish-ready frames to social media before the next at-bat. The whole method transfers to any sideline.

item.title: The $549 f/2.8 Zoom That Makes APS-C Feel Like a Pro System
item.description: Tamron just shipped a $549 f/2.8 zoom for Sony, Canon, Fujifilm, and Nikon crop-sensor cameras. It weighs 305 grams, focuses with a fast linear motor, and stays at f/2.8 through the whole range, the single upgrade that teaches an APS-C shooter more about exposure than any body ever will.

item.title: The Photo That Won Wildlife Photographer of the Year Is About Grief, Not Gear
item.description: The 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year grand title went to Federico Veronesi's black-and-white image of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf in Namibia. He found the family by reading drag marks in a dry riverbed, a reminder that the best wildlife photography is fieldcraft first and camera second.

item.title: Apple Built a Quantum-Proof Way to Prove a Photo Is Real. Here Is How It Works
item.description: Apple introduced Apple Reference Image, an opt-in mode on the iPhone 18 Pro that cryptographically signs raw pixel data at the sensor, before the operating system can touch it. It is a harder answer to the deepfake question than C2PA, and it is about to reshape what proof a photograph can carry.

item.title: Getty Is Going Private Through Bankruptcy. Here Is What Photographers Should Do Now
item.description: Getty Images announced a prepackaged Chapter 11 restructuring that would take the company private, backed by up to $533 million in new equity. Getty says there is no anticipated impact on contributors, but nothing is court-approved yet, and photographers who earn from stock should document what they are owed starting now.

item.title: The Gas Station You Drive Past Every Day Is a Photograph Waiting for Night
item.description: Fstoppers argues daylight documents a place while night light transforms it, and that darkness is the best background remover a photographer has. Expose for the highlights, set the white balance by hand, and scout without the camera.

item.title: The One Slider Move That Makes a Sunset Glow in Lightroom
item.description: Fstoppers follows Christian Möhrle's sunset edit: raising blacks inside a feathered mask creates the glow that exposure would blow out, while restrained color and a low denoise setting keep the file clean. The trick copies what a diffusion filter does, without the commitment.

item.title: Your Camera's Sensor Is Colorblind. Here Is How It Fakes Color
item.description: Fstoppers explains that every photosite on your sensor is a grayscale light meter, and color arrives through a 1975 Kodak patent: the Bayer mosaic, half green to match human vision. Demosaicing then rebuilds two-thirds of every pixel, which is why raw files look different in every converter.

item.title: Nikon Stripped a $3,000 Win Over AI, and It Changes the Rules for Everyone
item.description: Nikon disqualified the winning video in its Small World in Motion competition after judges found it broke the no-AI rule. The message for every photographer entering contests: read the fine print, keep your raw files, and know where your editing tools stop being allowed.

item.title: Is There Such a Thing as Bad Light in Street Photography?
item.description: Peter Forsgard says good light is a sedative for your visual instincts and that flat gray days expose whether a street photo has a story at all. If you only shoot in golden light, the gray months ahead are your test.

item.title: How to Tell a Beauty Dish From a Softbox Just by Looking at the Photo
item.description: Karl Taylor demonstrates how to read a portrait like a forensic scene: shadows reveal the light's position, skin specularity reveals the modifier, and falloff reveals the distance. Once you can read it, any image you admire becomes a diagram you can rebuild.

item.title: Canon's Phone App Is One of the Best. That Bar Is Low.
item.description: DPReview tested Canon's Camera Connect app on iOS and Android. It is one of the better camera apps, with quirks on both platforms, and the best trick is a USB cable.

item.title: Take Fewer Photos. See More.
item.description: James Popsys cut his daily shooting from thousands of frames to 250 on a Greenland trip and brought home better work. The cheapest cost of a frame is culling it.

item.title: Tamron's 20-40mm f/2.8 Comes to Nikon Z
item.description: Tamron's compact 20-40mm f/2.8 wide zoom arrives for Nikon Z on October 22 for $729, giving full-frame shooters a light, fast wide-to-normal zoom with an unusual range.

item.title: Camera Raw's New Grid View Is the Catalog-Free Workflow You Already Own
item.description: Adobe added a grid view with ratings and filters to Camera Raw, plus exposure matching that reads your camera's ambient light data — no Lightroom catalog required.

item.title: Sigma's 50-120mm f/2.8 Is the APS-C Zoom We've Been Waiting For
item.description: Sigma's new 50-120mm f/2.8 gives APS-C shooters a 390-gram, $799 portrait-and-events zoom, completing an affordable constant-aperture trio.

item.title: Parents Are Using AI for School Photos Instead of Photographers
item.description: Parents are using AI to turn plain-backdrop snapshots into school portraits, skipping the $25-$60 print package. 58% of U.K. photographers say they have lost commissioned work to AI.

item.title: Two Companies Now Ship Twice as Many Cameras as the Entire Mirrorless Market
item.description: IDC's numbers show DJI and Insta360 together ship more than twice as many cameras as all mirrorless makers combined — while mirrorless itself holds steady, selling fewer bodies at higher prices.

item.title: A Free RAW Editor That Teaches You How to Edit
item.description: Aftershoot launched Photon, a free RAW editor with an AI Coach that explains why each adjustment matters — built for photographers who shoot RAW but never learned what the sliders do.

item.title: Speed in a Photograph Is About Perception, Not Shutter Speed
item.description: Aviation photographer Simone Marulli says capturing speed starts with energy, not settings — the aircraft's angle, its position in the frame, and the tension in its wings do the storytelling.

item.title: Why Your Prints Never Match Your Screen — and How to Fix It
item.description: A monitor makes light; paper reflects it. The fix is a small chain of translations — a calibrated monitor, soft proofing, and one color manager, never two.

item.title: Is It Time to Upgrade Your Camera? A Marsh Test Answers It
item.description: Omar Gonzalez took a 2018 Fujifilm X-H1 into a marsh to ask the honest question: does fighting old gear make you better, or does it just cost you shots?

item.title: Canon, Nikon, Sony and Fujifilm Each See Your Future Differently
item.description: Nikkei asked all four camera giants where photography is headed. Canon bets on the shooting experience, Nikon on cascading flagship tech down, Sony on Spatial AI, Fujifilm on the joy of the dial.

item.title: Your Rim Light Isn't Weak — Your Fill Is Just Winning
item.description: Lighting educator Karl Taylor shows why two studio lights pull against each other in a high-key portrait, and the stop-by-stop method for balancing rim and fill.

item.title: Nikon's Z5IIC Drops the Viewfinder — Should You?
item.description: Nikon just cut the electronic viewfinder out of its cheapest full-frame camera and called it the Z5IIC. Here is what is gone, what survived, and whether the savings are worth it.

item.title: The Fastest Tilt-Shift Ever Is a 24mm f/2 From Laowa
item.description: Venus Optics' new Laowa 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift claims the speed crown for tilt-shift lenses, launches November 5, and is priced at $1,249.

item.title: Why f/16 Makes Every Photo a Little Softer
item.description: Diffraction is the one blur no lens can outrun. Here is how much sharpness f/16 actually costs, why there is no magic cliff, and when to stop down anyway.

item.title: Photoshop Can Now Move the Light in Your Photo
item.description: Relight, currently in Photoshop beta, lets you reposition, soften, and recolor the lighting in a finished photo. Here is what it does well and where it falls apart.

item.title: Twenty Years of Fall Color, One Shot List
item.description: Photographer Kate Garibaldi spent twenty Octobers learning that great fall photography is not about peak color. It is about the shot list you bring.

item.title: Top-Flight Football on an Entry-Level Camera
item.description: Photography student Chantelle Cook shadowed Motherwell FC's club photographer with her Canon EOS R50 and came home with pro-worthy shots. The three autofocus settings that made the difference.

item.title: Shoot Every Landscape Three Times: Wide, Medium, Close
item.description: A filmmaker's coverage trick, one wide, one medium, one close, turns a single sunrise location into a full sequence. Here is the three-frame exercise worth stealing.

item.title: What f/1.2 Actually Buys You After Dark
item.description: Nikon's three f/1.2 primes each weigh more than a kilogram. Night shooter Jack Wang tested them against their f/1.8 siblings, and the real lesson is not about light at all.

item.title: A 35mm Lens That Shoots Life-Size Macro. With Autofocus.
item.description: Laowa's new Acris 35mm F2.8 is the first wide-angle macro lens with autofocus \u2014 $449, and a lesson in how wide-angle macro changes the shot.

item.title: What Happens When You Take One Lens on a Trip
item.description: A photographer packed three lenses and shot with one. The case for the single-prime month \u2014 and why fixed-lens cameras keep selling out.

item.title: Stop Making One Lightroom Catalog Per Session
item.description: A 12-year wedding photographer runs one catalog per year. Why your catalog setup decides how fast you can find anything \u2014 and what Lightroom's backup actually backs up.
